Mr. Chairman, may I rise on a point of order. I do not think the hon. member for Timiskaming was trespassing beyond his time or over-stretching the patience of the committee. I am sure we would all like to hear him complete his speech, if Your Honour would be pleased to recognize the hon. member for Meadow Lake afterwards.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must have the unanimous consent of the committee to let the hon. member continue his remarks.
Agreed.

I will not abuse the privilege. I was only making an impassioned plea on behalf of the farmers who I believe have a different type of problem from that of other people. They have never budgeted for lawyers fees, for accountants fees or for bookkeeper's fees. They are really not in a position to establish an accrual accounting system at this time. The minister is here, and I know he comes from a municipality which is surrounded by a rural area. I only suggest to him that we stand these other three sections and refer them to the Agriculture Committee for study. I mentioned that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had made representations. Other farm organizations also have made representations, all of which have hinged on these two or three particular problems. The solutions suggested have not been identical in each case but the representations have been sincere. I therefore ask the minister to give consideration to some study of the problem by the agriculture committee. We will be with this legislation for a long time. I am not suggesting we will be with the income tax bill as such for a long time, but that we will have to live with the income tax act for a long time.
I realize the government believes we should have larger, more economical farms. I also realize there is an advantage in having large, easy to understand units. I am sure, however, the government will also agree there is a large number of voters in this country who are either one generation removed from the farm, or who may even still be close to the rural economy, who believe there is a way of life in Canada in ownership of land which does not involve only the hobby farmer but which involves a way

of life which is to be protected. I therefore make the plea that the minister consider referring this to a committee where we can specifically hear people on the particular subjects of concern. It would even seem to me that if this section were omitted when the bill is passed that would not be too bad. We could use the exceptions which are already there and, for a period of time, give consideration to what the best method is to solve this problem. The minister may have a better suggestion, but I make the plea that at least he give consideration to our obtaining some information from the farm organizations themselves concerning what might be a more equitable farm tax structure, without at the same time making it more difficult and more expensive for people to carry on in medium and small-sized farms in Canada today. We should make it possible for those people to continue the normal way of life they have chosen.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to this debate with a great deal of interest. I could not help but note the manner in which the parliamentary secretary, who comes from that great cattle country in the Calgary area, answered the hon. member for Crowfoot this morning when he was speaking on the very important topic which we were debating at that time. I am sure that when he goes back to his constituency he will have a little explaining to do to some of the cattlemen in that great area where cattle have been produced for so long and so well. I believe the hon. member for Crowfoot made a very important point when he referred to the situation of the Canadian cattlemen as compared with the position of the cattlemen to the south, and the problems our cattlemen face which are not faced by cattlemen in the United States. He referred to climatic conditions and many other conditions such as population. We must be on a competitive basis. I certainly think that the hon. member for Crowfoot got right down to the meat of the problem which these cattlemen face.
We must have competition. I am glad we do have competition among the livestock people. This is what the livestock men have fought for through the years. This is what they want to see continue. I believe the government was very lax in studying the situation of the United States cattlemen with regard to the basic herd. Since the government has not looked into this, I think that instead of standing only section 29 we should stand also sections 28, 30 and 31. If we stand one section, I believe we should stand all four sections because they are all very much connected. If we are to scrap the basic herd concept-and this has been talked about-then we might just as well scrap a good many of the livestock men because they will be forced out of business altogether. We might stop and think about the amount of money the various provincial governments have lent, for the purpose of setting up young farmers in areas which are adaptable to livestock production. For the life of me I do not understand, when we have the provincial governments trying to do something about keeping these boys and girls on the farms and providing them with a low rate of interest in order to get set up, why the federal government should be putting on this squeeze.
I am sure many of these people would not be very interested in continuing much further because it is
November 9, 1971

already very difficult for them to become established on a farm. After taking a good look at the situation, I cannot understand why this government would come in with such a bill. I do not think the government is listening to the people or is paying attention to what is going on in respect of the farm population. I would have thought the government would have given much more study to this matter. When one looks at the farming situation today, it is evident that farmers have not been able to pay the minimum wage. I think this is a shame.
I do not understand why farmers should not be able to pay the minimum wage and thereby be in line with those enterprises which they have been instrumental in establishing in the first place. For instance, why should not the livestock man or the farmer be able to pay the same wages that are paid by telephone companies, power companies and highway construction companies. The farmers are the people who were instrumental in bringing about these developments. Now, they find themselves in a predicament. We talk about unemployment. It is terrible to think of the number of people who are unemployed.
If you go to a farm or to a ranch and try to hire a man you will see what you are up against, because in some provinces what farmers are getting for their produce does not even provide them with a minimum wage. I think this is a shame and the government should take a good, hard look at these provisions before they talk about what they will do with the basic herd concept.
Farmers find themselves in a predicament. I made a check on this in my own district very recently-and it is a pretty good district. In certain sections of that country I could scarcely find a farmer who could make a go of it unless he was subsidizing his holdings through some other method-his wife was teaching, nursing or working in other ways to help subsidize the farm or the farmer was moonlighting, driving a school bus, doing construction work or some other work in order to keep his farm together. If the government does not know this, it should take a look at the situation. Very few small farmers today can make a go of it without subsidizing their farms. This should not be the case.
If this bill passes, farmers will be driven off their farms, and I think this is a shame. I have taken a good look at what is going on in the farming community and I find that the trouble lies in the fact that farmers are forced to produce at lower prices than have prevailed for years. You get 60 cents for barley, 40 cents for oats and $1.20 for No. 3 wheat. This is what the farmer is up against. This government will make it utterly impossible for him to stay on his farm. I cannot for the life of me understand why the government does not listen to the people and find out what is going on. People in Saskatchewan made their opinions known last night. The government should take a good look at the situation before coming in with a bill such as this.
I believe that the basic herd concept has been set up by regulation. I am not sure that it has been set up under the act. I think the four sections should be stood. They should be sent back to the committee on agriculture for further recommendations. It is a waste of time for us to sit here and debate such a bill, and it is almost impossible for the
Income Tax Act
House to pass these provisions on farm taxation. If these sections are sent to committee, the committee might come up with a sound report and we might find out what the basic herd concept really means. Many of the basic herds that have been set up are registered herds. Many young people who in the past few years have been starting out in the farming business have not been able to establish a basic herd, and they will be very disappointed. I do not know why they should want to carry on and I do not understand why the government would not want to do something about this problem. They will find that these provisions will destroy many pure-bred herds.
I should like to make a few remarks regarding the capital gains tax on used machinery. We must take into account the cost of new machinery now as compared with what it was three or four years ago. If a farmer has to pay capital gains tax when he trades old machine for new machinery, at a time when he must pay almost twice as much for a new machine, I do not see how he will ever be able to buy machinery for farming.
We do not need to confine ourselves to the Prairie. Let us consider any rural area and we will see how disappointing it is for the sons and daughters of farmers to be unable to carry on the family farm. It is next to impossible and I do not know how many will be able to do it. Several provincial governments are trying to help out farmers in this situation, but here we have the federal government wrecking the whole works in trying to bring in a bill such as this.
I do not see any point to standing only section 29. I believe the four sections should be stood because they are related to each other. I do not know where the government thinks it is going with this kind of legislation affecting the farming population of Canada.
Would the hon. member allow a question?

Yes, Mr. Chairman.

I would ask the hon. member for Meadow Lake a question with reference to the basic herd. What is the difference between a young couple who are being helped by the provincial government and his own situation on the farm, where he has a large herd of cattle? In other words, the hon. member has a large stock of cattle, while the young couple has not yet established one. Could the hon. member explain the difference between his case and that of the young couple?

Yes. There is no difference, because my farm could not carry on if it were not for my sons whom I want to set up. There is no difference at all between the young couple who get a loan from the provincial govern-
9490

November 9, 1971
Income Tax Act
ment and my sons who receive my assistance in setting up a farm.

I do not want to take up too much time today because yesterday I made some comments with reference to these items. However, there are one or two matters on which I should like to seek the advice of the parliamentary secretary. One of them arises from the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which contains a section headed "Guidance to the farmer". It reads:
The problems for the farmer in dealing efficiently with the problems he faces in the period of transition to the provisions of the new bill will be very real, and it is important that he be as fully aware as possible of what he should do to set his records in proper order, and in all other respects arrange his affairs to his best advantage. The problems involved in establishing valuation day records of assets, and valuations on them, are one example here.
We very much approve the government's intent to prepare working guides to aid taxpayers in such problems. These should be clear in layman's terms and widely distributed.
I hope the government takes note of the words "These should be clear in layman's terms," because that is the difficulty with this bill. It is very complicated for the ordinary individual, and in fact many of us in the House of Commons have great difficulty with it and are not sure that we understand it.
One should be prepared, we believe, directed to the specific problems of farmers.
I presume this one has been prepared, but I wonder whether during its preparation the farming organizations were asked for their advice. They are the representatives of the farmers. I would think that before a pamphlet such as is described here is sent to farmers, the farm organizations should have an opportunity to examine it and determine whether it does the job it is supposed to do.
Although section 29 has been stood, there are one or two questions about it that still perturb me. There are matters the government should take note of when deciding what to do about the section. Earlier today the hon. member for Simcoe North talked about people who raise special breeding herds to be sold for breeding stock. From time to time we hear about people who have developed outstanding animals. I have a particular interest in this matter.
One of my constituents has been breeding Charolais cattle-in fact two people have been doing so-and just the other day one of those cattle was sold for $53,000. No doubt the income tax people have already heard about it. I wonder what the provisions in this bill would do to an individual like that, who spends a lot of time raising pure-bred stock and eventually has the satisfaction of going to a sale and getting a price-not always as high as the one I have mentioned-for an animal to which he has given great attention, keeping records of blood lines and doing all the things that lead to good breeding. This is a special case. There is another special case that should be considered. As I mentioned yesterday, there is the case of the junior farmer or 4-H club member who is given an animal each spring to rear and who sells it at a fall fair. Representatives of packing companies attend the fall fairs and bid on such animals. Generally the young person gets more than the market value of the animal. But there is one particular case that has come to my attention.

Young people have won what we call the Queen's Guineas at the Royal Winter Fair in Toronto. I am not sure how much that amounts to in cash, but I well remember that some years ago a steer that won the Queen's Guineas at the Royal Winter Fair was sold for about $5 a pound on the hoof. Such animals are bought by firms such as Simpsons, Eatons or meat packing companies, for promotional purposes. Sold at that price, the cash realization, taking into account the value of the prize, was around $7,000 or $8,000. Such things have to be taken into consideration when examining this bill.
My hon. friend from Meadow Lake and other hon. members have argued that all these sections dealing with agriculture should be stood. Personally, I do not know why this voluminous bill was brought in at this time and why a deadline was set to get it through by the end of this year. After all, it will affect the lives of practically everybody in Canada. It is important to a great many people. So far as many of us can see, only those people who will receive increased income tax exemptions and who will be taken off the income tax rolls will benefit from it. But probably by the time the bill goes through and is enacted the cost of living will have increased to such an extent that their so-called savings will have melted away.
Therefore I would add my voice to those who are suggesting that not only should these sections be stood for the time being and sent to a committee for further consideration, but I think more time should be taken to examine all sections of the bill to ensure that when it is passed it will represent the best job that can be done on tax reform.

Mr. Chairman, for the next few minutes I will not engage in small talk on farming but deal with large philosophical questions. That will give Canadian Press a chance to go out and have a glass of water until approximately 5.27 p.m., since I became dead in their eyes as the result of a speech I made last week in this debate.
I would like to make one remark and raise several questions regarding this part of the debate. This arises out of the fact that as I travel through part of my constituency I am struck by the number of small farm places that have been vacated. In other words, I am struck by the death of small farming operations in my part of Canada. I believe that this sort of thing is also happening in other parts of the country.
To establish the bona fides for my remarks let my say that none of my ancestors for at least two generations of which I am aware, nor I myself, has been qualified to run a farm-and if we attempted to do so we would immediately find ourselves in great peril. So I am not posing as an expert on the death of the small farm, but I am posing perhaps as a philosopher on the question of why this sort of thing should happen. In East Hants one can see a prosperous community of farms and also many farms that have been vacated. Therefore we know that the institution of the small farm is imperilled.
Mr. Chairman, it is very difficult to gather one's thoughts when there is such a babble from the backbenches on the other side, even though it does not appear on the record. There is one question I wish to ask the parliamentary secretary. Granted that a new income tax act should not only be a document of reform to overcome some of the problems I have mentioned on about 15 or 20
November 9, 1971

occasions in this debate-it should also be a document to point the way to the future.
From the philosophical point of view, I wonder if the parliamentary secretary or the minister could tell us whether there is anything in this document which tends to save the small farming operation in Canada. Frankly, I do not think there is. But perhaps there was some good intention which was lost in the discussions and which would show that our children and grandchildren could adopt farming as a way of life. I think I should have first put the question: Is there any way that one would be encouraged to establish a farm? The second question would be: Will there be any incentive to operate a small farm unit?
These are basic questions and I do not think we have the answers. We have been dealing with questions regarding farming operations of monumental size, but if we are to establish some sort of equity in taxation we should also establish a policy with regard to what we want to build in Canada. When I drive down the highway for about 20 miles in East Hants and see 40 or 50 vacant farm buildings, I must ask the question here and I think I should have an answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a number of questions have been raised by hon. members. I am sorry that the hon. member for Central Nova was not able to remain, because he asked some of them. However, most dealt with appeal, enforcement and administration sections of the bill rather than those currently under consideration, so perhaps an opportunity will arise to respond to the hon. member when those sections are before us. I do not think I should take the time of the committee now to respond to them, since he is -not here. However, I should like to congratulate him on the fruits of his own research as opposed to that of the research department referred to earlier.
During the afternoon there have been a number of suggestions that something could be accomplished by referring these sections-not just section 29 but others-to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I think hon. members opposite are doing a disservice to committee of the whole which is charged with the responsibility of dealing with this bill, and also to the work of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Over a long period of time the latter committee heard representations from agricultural organizations and individuals concerned about agriculture and had the opportunity to report and make recommendations.
The hon. member for Battle River was very active in this regard, as was the hon. member for Dauphin and the hon. member for Regina East who served full-time on that committee. They are men with an agricultural background. In addition, on a number of occasions we were honoured with the presence of the hon. member for Kent-Essex, and on one or two occasions we even had the hon. member for Crowfoot join us when matters of particular interest to him were being considered.

When time permitted.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite, as well as those from this side of the House who served well on the committee, had opportunities to advance the views they are now advancing. The Finance Committee has done its work and nothing useful would be served by agreeing to the suggestion that has been made.
The hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Water-loo was not able to remain for the answers to his questions, but perhaps he will read Hansard. I should point out that the area of information services to which he was alluding is the function of the Department of National Revenue which will be bringing forth various publications for the guidance of taxpayers under the new system. Accordingly, the hon. member might wish to raise that matter with the Minister of National Revenue, but I seriously doubt that the Department of National Revenue will be in a position to finalize the material until Parliament has passed Bill C-259 and it has become law.
The question of the desirability of this information getting into the hands of taxpayers might impress itself on all members of the House. I very much agree with the hon. member that it is desirable that taxpayers be informed very soon, and in layman's language, of the best way to adapt, where necessary, their business practice to the requirements of the new system. Until that time comes I think it would be regrettable if many taxpayers who do not already find that their business affairs require them to rely on professional tax advisers paid money to people currently advertising their services in anticipation of the forthcoming tax system. Until the tax bill becomes law, those tax advisers are not in a very good position to give concrete advice on matters of real application under the forthcoming law.
I reiterate that I hope the general body of taxpayers does not take the bait of the many advertisements that are appearing on a "scare" basis inviting them to spend money in anticipation on a bill that has not passed Parliament. The Department of National Revenue will be making a real effort to give explanatory material in layman's language which will, hopefully, eliminate the necessity for professional tax advice for all but the small minority of taxpayers who now find themselves in need of that kind of advice. I thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity to put that comment on the record. The hon. member went on to raise the question of breeding stock which had also been raised by the hon. member for Simcoe North. Rather than repeat that answer, and as he is absent, I would refer to the answer I gave the hon. member for Simcoe North.
The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants invited me to participate in this debate on a philosophical basis. Mr. Chairman, I have enough trouble trying to do what I think I am competent to do without discussing agriculture on a philosophical plane.
You are wise there.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to pose a few brief questions with regard to section 28. The parliamentary secretary tended to reject the concept of referring section 29 to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I do

not know whether he was going to refer section 29 or all these four sections to that committee, but he seemed to reject that idea. Perhaps when he rises again he could give the committee a preview of exactly what study will be given to section 29 now that it has been stood.
Surely they did not just stand it in order to enter it again in the same form. Surely they would like to convince us that they will thoroughly examine it to see whether it is detrimental to the industry. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has invited me to indicate what is the nature of the consideration that will be given to section 28 that was stood at the suggestion of the hon. member and with the agreement of hon. members on this side of the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would simply say that it seems appropriate for us to be given the opportunity to study the record of the debate on that section and the remarks made yesterday and today. As the hon. member is well aware, representations from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have recently been received and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association has been bringing its views forcibly to the attention of Members of Parliament. Obviously, I am not in a position to indicate, nor do I intend to convey the impression that I can indicate, what if any changes may result. Nor may I indicate any timing as to when possible changes might be expected.
The hon. member asked a question regarding section 28(4). I did not have the opportunity of reading that rather lengthy section while the hon. member was asking the question. I will take the opportunity to look at it and will try to respond to his question before six o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I have in my hand the brief of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. What strikes me about this presentation-and I am sure the parliamentary secretary will agree with me-is the very reasonable argument it puts forward. The cattlemen of Canada, among whom we may include mixed farmers who are in the beef industry, enjoy an enviable record. They have never come to the government hat in hand and asked for special consideration.
If you read this brief carefully-I am sure the parliamentary secretary has, although it was addressed to the

Minister of Finance-you will see that it is couched in the typical and modest understatements of the best cattle breeders and mixed farmers of Canada. They are not asking for special consideration. If you read the brief, however, it is plain that they are not overly happy about Bill C-259. I would put the last paragraph of the brief on record for the convenience of those who wish to refer to it. It reads:
However, this brief itself is not enough. We believe this issue is so important to agriculture that we herewith request an opportunity to meet with the proper authorities to discuss these matters and to offer more information if requested to support our case.
I do not hold myself out as an expert in the field of cattle breeding although I have had experience as a ranch-hand and was raised on a farm. I have lived with these people all my life. They are worried about the implications of Bill C-259. They are particularly concerned about those sections of the bill that affect agriculture. They ask, in which direction is agriculture going and what is to be the future of cattlemen and farmers in general?
Cattlemen are not confined to western Canada. I suggest that as many head of cattle are produced in other parts of Canada as are produced in western Canada. This question affects vitally the cattle breeders of Ontario, Quebec, the Maritimes and British Columbia. Thousands of cattle are raised in the Fraser Valley. If they are not raised, they are fattened. When you speak of the cattle industry you speak not only of the raising but of the fattening, improving, marketing and selling of cattle.
The Cattlemen's Association is worried about some of the implications of this bill. The question of the basic herd was thoroughly discussed and I was pleased that section 29 was stood. I hope it will be stood long enough to permit consultation to take place between those concerned and the government. We want no more short cuts, no matter how well meaning they may be. We want no more talk about ministers being ready to go to jail, and all sorts of horrible consequences that may follow if one breaks the law. We want to make sure that the law as passed has been brought into being through full consultation with people whose living and future depend on our doing a good job with this bill.
Hear, hear!

Nothing is more serious to the people of Alberta than any infringement upon the rights of cattlemen and mixed farmers to stay on their farms and run them in their own way. I say what Mark Antony said to the crowd: If I am wrong, I apologize: however, I am sure I am right.
Every part of this brief is couched in the typical understatement of outdoor men, men who are not self-conscious, who are not worried about petty things but who are worried about their basic freedoms and their right to remain free and independent. They do not like coming to the government and asking for special consideration. These men believe-I say this with great conviction-that every Member of Parliament believes in supporting their basic freedoms. They expect to be treated as fairly and as equitably as every Canadian expects to be treated.
These people are capable of producing the finest beef cattle in the world. They are a great credit to their profes-
November 9, 1971

sion and to their personal integrity, ambition and labour. They know their profession-and beef raising in Canada can qualify as a profession. These men are not merely entrepreneurs; they are experts. They do not dabble in this field. They produce the finest range cattle in Canada. They will put on your plate the finest beef that is to be found anywhere-good Canadian beef steak. In their own mild way they say they want to be consulted. They do not say, "We demand this." They want to be consulted, as they have a right to expect. As far as every member of my party is concerned, we will make sure that they are consulted.
As I said, I am not an expert on beef raising. Those in the Canadian Cattlemen's Association are experts in this field. They have taken the trouble of consulting among themselves in order to bring forward the short and concise document we have before us. This must be considered if common sense is to apply to sections of the act relating directly to this association. If we do not do that, we are delinquent.
The hon. member for Crowfoot is to be congratulated on making such a strong presentation that the government has seen fit to stand section 29. This brief should be carefully read-the last paragraph in particular-because it contains very detailed and precise information which the government requires before these sections of the bill can be included in a permanent income tax act which will be equitable to cattlemen. In the brief they say their concern about Bill-259 derives from insufficient evidence being given to the unique and special nature of farming. I have said this before and the hon. member for Crowfoot and others on this side of the House have said it in no uncertain terms.
Farming is not just another business. It is a way of life. On the farm you do not punch a clock or count the hours. Anyone not engaged in the process of raising beef does not know how many unpaid hours a cowboy works. If a cow becomes sick in the middle of the night or is having a calf, the cowboy is up all night. He must act as a midwife and a nurse. His hours are not cut off by a union time-clock. If he is worth his salt-and he normally is-he is on duty 24 hours a day. You cannot define that in terms of union wages.
The whole family is involved in the process of raising cattle. I have seen a housewife wrap her coat around a calf, put the calf behind the stove and feed it with her child's bottle. She cares for it until it is able to stand and return to its mother in the barn. What in this act gives recognition to this different and special nature of farming? Is it a capital gain when you raise a small herd and produce the finest beef in the world? Is it a capital gain, or is it a question of deferred wages for the whole family? The housewife on the farm often rides out on the range to help her husband round up the cattle. She has no relief from taxation. The husband has no relief from taxation in the normal sense of the word.
Today we are all involved in seeking security and perhaps rightly so. Where does the family farmer and rancher stand with regard to the Canada Pension Plan? As the Minister of Finance and all members know, you cannot join the Canada Pension Plan unless you show a net profit
Income Tax Act
on your farm or ranch. How many small farmers or ranchers have the know-how or can afford to keep proper books? Of these, how many earn $800 after expenses are paid? That is the minimum amount necessary to join the Canada Pension Plan. Even the maximum pension is not magnificent, yet you have to show at least $4,700 net profit. That would be an exception.
It is true that some ranchers in western Canada show considerable profit, but we are talking about averages. We in this House make rules for the average Canadian, the small farmer, the small rancher and the average person who started off with a quarter section of land and no money. After a lifetime on the land, they may have built up a big spread. I repeat, this is only deferred wages.
You don't know what you are talking about.

Someone has said I do not know what I am talking about. I have the scars of labour on my body to show that I know what I am talking about. I worked on a homestead. It required a great deal of work.
In western Canada there are many broken farms and broken lives. These people have put 20 or 30 years into working hard on the farm. They have received very little in the way of monetary return. They receive some reward, the freedom of being their own boss. They have received a reward by changing a bog, sandhill or a piece of stony ground into a viable farm. This is not capital gains; it is deferred wages-small wages at that.
Some couples have worked hard for 40 years on a quarter section of land which is stony, bony and full of stumps. They have drained it, cared for it, fertilized, seeded and harvested it. They had to borrow the money and had to pay excess prices for freight rates on farm machinery. They have received depressed prices for their product. An improvement from a $10 quarter section to a $50,000 viable farm is not a capital gain. That is utter and ridiculous nonsense. I do not know how anyone could say this is all wages or all capital gains. I would hate to have to do that job. This is unfair to those who took a raw quarter section of land and made it into a viable farm. They have already paid for it with blood, sweat and tears. They spent many hours of long, hard work during the cold Canadian winters. They put their lives into this investment, yet there are those who say this is a capital gain.
The members of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association are heroic people. They do not want to be called heroes. They want to be left alone to run their operations. When they pay for a farm with labour and deferred wages, they want the right to leave it to their children or grandchildren, unencumbered by unnecessary taxation.
My friends to the left, who are avowed socialists, say that this bill is too socialistic for them. It has an air of compulsion about it that they do not like. They are to be commended for this. This is a form of compulsion by taxation. In a great many cases it is confiscation by taxation. The Canadian Cattlemen's Association does not shriek independence or secession. They have thought about it but that is not the way they behave. They spend too much time working to sit around and talk about revolution. They want evolution. They want us to work

November 9, 1971
Income Tax Act
out a square deal for them. Even if they do not say what is equitable, it is up to us to determine this for them. Many provisions in this bill are not equitable. It is not equitable to treat farming like every other profession in this country. It is not the same.
Farmers do not have union hours or fair employment practices. They do not have equal treatment of women. I should like to see the women of this country get up and talk about that. I should like to see them get behind the housewife on the farm and ask for a fair deal for these women.
.50 p.m.)
Would you like me to talk about child labour for a while? Have you any idea of the kind of labour a child often puts in on the farm, unpaid except for bare grub? And they are leaving the farms in droves. Not only are their parents incapable of making a living under present conditions, but when a greedy government comes along intent on treating deferred wages as a capital gain, saying, "We want our share," it is no wonder they decide not to continue as their parents have done, breaking their backs to improve stony land. I do not think the government should have any part of it.
But I go along with the brief the Canadian Cattlemen's Association has presented. They ask to be treated as gentlemen. There is no word in their brief of revolution or secession. There is just a plea for equity. It is not equity to take deferred wages and call it capital. The farmers have paid with their labour for every dollar which has gone through their hands. They have paid in higher freight rates, in a lower standard of living, in their employment of other people, in their production of the finest food of any country in the world. I am thinking now about beef, although I might say the same about wheat and about a great many other Canadian agricultural products. As I say, we have been asked to consider a gentlemanly and mild brief from this organization. The plea it contains is: Do not act further until you have held the kind of consultations which this government has always claimed to support.
The government opposite is not the first which has consulted the people. But if this is their boast, and if they intend to put it into action, I beg them to take this brief and give it the consideration which has been requested. There is no rush. Canadian cattlemen and ranchers have been in existence for 100 years. There is no rush to get this bill through in the next three weeks. These people will not be satisfied unless they are consulted. It will not be good enough for us to sit down in the absence of consultation and make rules to govern members of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, tie up their assets, take away their land and restrict their ability to build up basic herds. I remind the committee that the record of these people is excellent.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but I do so because his time has expired.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I undertook to respond to the question asked by the hon. member for Crowfoot regarding section 28(4). That provision applies where a farmer who has reported his income on a cash basis leaves Canada and becomes a non-resident. It operates, in

effect, to put him on an accrual basis at the time of his departure so that cash receipts attributable to his period of operation of the farm business prior to giving up residence become taxable. Under the general Canadian tax law personal taxation is levied on the basis of residence but cash receipts after the farmer has left Canada attributable to business operations carried on while he was resident here are properly taxable.
Are they charged against the land he left, or would the government search him out wherever he might be?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think other countries would necessarily enforce the act for us, but any taxes due would be chargeable against whatever assets he left in Canada including any interest he might have in any land.
If he had sold the land, would the new owner have to discharge the liability for tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, there is no lien on the property of anybody else but it is possible, of course, that there might be a balance payable to him under a mortgage, and that could be attached. But nobody else would be called upon to pay the revenue department any money which was not owed the taxpayer.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: I notice the parliamentary secretary said it would be the same as the accrual method. According to the section as I read it, the assets which this individual possessed in terms of land or livestock or grain, particularly under the accrual method, would go into inventory. Would the total amount be taxable in that year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: To the extent that it was inventory it would be income for the year. But there are, of course, provisions for reserves. Is the hon. member speaking of the non-resident in this case?

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Then we are not dealing specifically with the person who has given up Canadian residence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. As the committee will recall, on Friday last the Chair raised a question as to the procedural acceptability of the motion proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West to amend section 74. It might be helpful if at this point the Chair mentioned that at the time of the adjournment at six o'clock this evening it was agreed, by special arrangement made earlier this day, that the committee would proceed to the consideration of sections previously under consideration. If hon. members would like me to put them on the record, the sections the committee now has before it are 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 81, 126, 144, 145, 148, 149,198, 199, 200 to 207, 248 to 252 and 254.
As I have said, when the committee last considered this grouping the hon. member for Edmonton West proposed an amendment to section 74 in respect of which amendment the Chair expressed some doubt as to its procedural acceptability. Unless other hon. members wish to be of assistance on the question of its procedural acceptability, the Chair is prepared to make a ruling now on the amendment.
I took under advisement the amendment moved last Friday by the hon. member for Edmonton West. The effect of the amendment, if passed, would be to shift the incidence of taxation from one taxpayer to another. It seems to me that it would little matter that the financial initiative of the Crown permits it to initiate a taxation proposal if it were then open to any hon. member to propose, by way of amendment, a different substantive scheme of his own. In his argument on the procedural aspect of the amendment, the hon. member for Edmonton West referred to the altering of the balance of ways and means. I indicated that my concern was whether the amendment would shift the incidence of taxation and later the hon. member for Edmonton West was kind enough to direct his remarks to that point.
At the outset I should mention that an alteration in the balance of ways and means has not been a factor in decisions made to date in this committee. It seems to me that in modern day practice it is impossible for any hon. member to move an amendment on a taxation matter that would not affect the balance of ways and means. If this were the only consideration to be applied in determining the procedural acceptability of a motion, I would think that in this day and age no motion could successfully pass the test. Here I should like to refer to Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, citation 268, and read it into the record:
Income Tax Act
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, example of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals tor the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as an alternative duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the Crown.
(2) An amendment proposing to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property, as an alternative for inhabited house duty imposed by resolution has been admitted.
Hon. members who are familiar with this citation will know that the authority quoted for that statement dates back to 1852 and 1853, and also the next statement, "See also similar proposal to substitute a duty on soap for a duty on newspapers". It seems to the Chair that the authority on which this citation is founded pre-dates confederation. I emphasize the latter part of the citation because it seems to me that it is an authority which must be of importance to us in considering the matter before us. That authority, in the latter part, reads as follows:
According to modern practice such an amendment is out of order. Even if the exact equivalence in the amount of the yield could be guaranteed (which is manifestly impossible), the objective that the incidence of the tax proposed would be extended to persons previously exempt would be fatal to such an amendment.
On October 25, 1971, at page 9013 of Hansard, in considering the amendment then proposed by the hon. member for Portneuf I stated that the Chair must first preserve the principle of the financial initiative of the Crown. On two or three occasions during the proceedings on this bill the Chair accepted amendments which purported to reduce taxation across the board in a general way.
On those occasions citation 265, paragraph (1) of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition was used as an authority. On the other hand, the proposed amendments which have been disallowed by the Chair, including the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Portneuf, were proposals which on the one hand reduced taxation but which on the other hand attempted to shift the incidence of taxation. It was the latter aspect, in these cases, which the Chair was unable to reconcile with the principle of the financial initiative of the Crown as stated in paragraph 2 of citation 263 of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition. That citation reads as follows:
The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a minister of the Crown, unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of Parliament; nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the Crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition. In like manner, no increase can be considered either of an existing, or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister, acting on behalf of the Crown; nor can a member other than a minister move for the introduction of a bill framed to effect a reduction of duties, which would incidentally effect the increase of an existing duty, or the imposition of a new tax, although the aggregate amount of imposition would be diminished by the provisions of the bill.

November 9, 1971
Income Tax Act
It seems to me that the hon. member's proposed amendment would inevitably shift the incidence of tax as between spouses and undoubtedly in many cases would increase the tax of one of the parties. I should like to assure the hon. member for Edmonton West that I have carefully reviewed the ruling of Mr. Speaker on December 11, 1969, as the hon. member asked me to do and to which he referred in his argument. With respect, that precedent is not analogous to the situation now before the committee. It seems to me that what the hon. member for Edmonton West attempted to do on that occasion was to introduce a flat fee basis for a transportation tax which would provide an equivalent return to and in lieu of the tax provided for in the bill.
In the case before the committee, I suggest no equivalency in return is being sought. But here again, as in the precedent cited, there would be a shifting of the incidence of taxation. In the case before us the hon. member would initiate or increase a tax for persons not now subject to tax. I realize, of course, that there would also be a decrease in taxes for other taxpayers. The decrease in total might well be greater than the increase. In any event, there is no suggestion that they would be equivalent. Having made the distinction, it seems to me I do not need to consider at this time whether the citation in May is based on a well founded precedent.
With respect to the comments of the hon. member for Peace River on the proposed amendment as it applies to subsection (5), it seems to me that the Crown has set forth in that subsection a proposal to impose taxation in certain cases. This is a statement of the financial initiative of the Crown. If the purpose of subsection (5) is to provide the Crown, through a minister, a method of imposing taxation in certain cases, it is open to an hon. member to make an across the board reduction in the rate of taxation, but it is not open to him to initiate a proposal which would shift the incidence of taxation which is implicit in the proposal of the Crown as set forth in subsection (5). For these reasons I must regretfully decline to put the motion moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West.

Mr. Chairman, of course I accept your ruling, although I am, if I may say so with respect, reserving my opinion with regard to its exact effect. With regard to whether Your Honour's ruling, I shall re-examine whether it conforms with the authorities, not Beauchesne-which I suggest is limited and somewhat dangerous on these particular points-but May where perhaps there are many authoritative sources of reference.
In any event, having established this point I will now look at the substance of the whole of section 74. My only regret in putting the amendment as I did is that I had not included subsection (4) of section 74 because that too is affected in part by the principle I am against. Outside of the fact that this has been a so-called rule-not quite from immemorial days because the Income Tax Act goes back to 1917 and I doubt very much whether this particular provision was one of those at that time-I wonder why in this day of changing social concepts with regard to this question, apart from, we might say, an ethereal sphere of abuse, there is the insistence at this point, with the consequences which I have raised, that in very legitimate cases for which the child care exemption, incidentally, was
[The Chairman.]
designed to provide, there is now to be a denial because of non-qualification or disentitlement under section 74(3) and the arguments I advanced the other day.
I would like to hear from the parliamentary secretary, since the whole thing is back on the table for re-enactment, why there is this particular insistence or objection to the points that I have raised and why the government would disentitle those people whom I have enumerated from the benefits of the child care provisions and the workers allowance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This question has been answered two or three times, obviously not to the satisfaction of the hon. member. The problem here involves opportunities for income splitting, which would not be equitable to taxpayers who are not self-employed and do not have that opportunity. In the opinion of the government it would be most unfair to open up this opportunity to self-employed people when it will be denied to people on salaries or wages.

May I point out, with the greatest respect, that the parliamentary secretary is comparing apples with oranges. We are not concerned here with people who are employed by others. I find the answer absolutely incomprehensible. This is no case of a wife who is an employee of her husband who is an employee of someone else. Why bring these people into the act? It is totally irrelevant to compare these people with those who are self-employed.
Take the case of the person who is the principal owner of a limited company, no different from the man across the street in the same type of business. Yet in the one case the wife who comes to work for the business-quite legitimately so-will be allowed all the advantages under the Income Tax Act that I have pointed out, while if the business is not incorporated the law says that the wife is not only not considered as a separate taxpayer but she is not a worker and is not entitled either to child care benefit or to workers allowance.
If the parliamentary secretary can say that there is no justification for that comparison, then he is welcome to it, but these self-employed people whom I have mentioned are no different from the man who owns three shares which control the small company, the other share being held by the lawyer to make it a private corporation. Remember that some of them are getting the benefits, and the individual who works as an employee suffers because his wife cannot get these benefits. If she is working for someone else, she will certainly be getting the benefits whether she is working in a company or a private business. She will get these benefits so long as there is not this husband and wife relationship.	.
What is even more nonsensical, if they are not husband and wife but have a common law relationship-the woman is the man's mistress-she will be entitled to collect whether the business is incorporated or whether it is a sole ownership. There again I wonder why this particular advantage should be granted. Or is it that this time the state does go into the bedrooms, because it certainly has gone into the bedrooms and it vouches for the credentials.
November 9, 1971

Mr. Chairman, we have been discussing this point for some time. This is one reason why the bill has been discussed for so long. This is a matter that will mean a great deal to small businessmen. It is incomprehensible to me why the parliamentary secretary should say that this will open a great door to misuse and that these people will do something very bad. Let him go down and meet some of these people. They are not crooks; they are people who are interested in paying their own way and in being good citizens. Did he discuss this provision with any small businessmen? I wonder whether any discussions have been held with the people who are involved.
Earlier today we were talking about the basic herd concept with regard to agricultural matters and we found that not too much discussion had taken place with agricultural organizations. Here we have a similar situation. I cannot see why the government cannot give in a little once in a while and make it possible for the small businessman or the small farmer whose wife works hard to keep him in business and off the welfare rolls so that he can be independent and run his own show in our free enterprise system.
I cannot for the life of me see that this would make much difference to the amount of money that this government would take because, after all, if a man pays his wife a wage he cannot claim her as an income tax exemption. I cannot see any reason for the stubbornness of the government in not giving in on this small point which could be so important to a great many people.

I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell us the estimates of the department regarding the amount of revenue that this possible loophole would create. I am wondering how much research has gone into the preparation of this section. Was it the type of research that was so evident this morning when the hon. member for Crowfoot was discussing the basic herd concept and the parliamentary secretary, with the Minister of Finance and with all the high-priced help they have around them- as was pointed out so well this morning-had not looked into the simple matter of comparing the ranchers' situation in Canada with that of our friends south of the border who are our competitors?
We heard the parliamentary secretary tell the hon. member for Crowfoot to keep his ears open as well as his mouth, but ten minutes later he came back to apologize to the House for having made a mistake. I was wondering whether the same kind of thought and research had gone into the section which we are considering so far as concerns the amount of revenue that this supposed loophole would create. It was certainly adequately pointed out the other day that this is merely a piece of legislation on morality, or immorality if you prefer, which would not allow a man and his wife to work as a team and to adjust their income in any way they see fit, to their advantage. This is a very important concept and I would like the parliamentary secretary to come forward with some estimate. I would like to find out what the department has done with regard to revenue estimates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter, as I explained a number of times on Friday and no doubt will have the
Income Tax Act
opportunity to explain a number of times before this evening is over, is not one of revenue: it is a matter of equity. I suppose a casual observer of this procedure- particularly referring to the very active part the hon. member for Battle River took in the deliberations of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs-could not help but remark on the amount of time being devoted during this procedure to matters that are carried over verbatim from the old act and do not involve changes or reform at all. It is really quite interesting to me to witness this particular procedure.
However, the question in this case is not one of revenue at all. It is simply one of equity and of not-I know the hon. member for Edmonton West appreciates the point- affording to self-employed people an opportunity for income splitting that is not available to other taxpayers.
That is a lot of nonsense. [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, is there such a difference between employing one's wife, son or daughter in any business? I think that the point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is perfectly valid. Why should employing the son or the daughter be different from employing the wife in a business run by the husband? Then why not exempt from tax the wife on the same basis as the daughter, the son, the nephew, the niece or any other relative?
Where is the difference? I would like to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) tell us how one can manage to be fair in income tax matters.
The hon. member for Edmonton West was perfectly right to raise that point and the parliamentary secretary ought to consider it. Why does he not consider it?

Mr. Chairman, I also want to ask a brief question of the parliamentary secretary, dealing with the same point. It appears that if there are two businesses operating side by side in a small town, and in each case the husband wants to employ his wife, her wages will not qualify as a business expense deduction for income tax purposes. But if two men decide to swap wives for business purposes, with each man hiring the other's wife, they will be money ahead because they can then have their wives file their own income tax returns. This is a ridiculous situation. I recognize that this is not a criticism of the legislation that is proposed but is a criticism of the law as it exists.
The government should give serious attention to this promotion of wife swapping for business purposes. It is an outrageous situation. I asked the parliamentary secretary a question the other day and he did not answer it. I asked him, was it correct that so far as the income tax laws are concerned the wife is really a nonentity. She is not considered as a human being when she works in her husband's store. She is in the class of a machine which fulfils a function but does not qualify for recognition as an employee. That is a very reprehensible kind of rule, one which any decent individual in a position of authority would be anxious to improve.
9498

November 9, 1971
Income Tax Act
I would like some explanation from the parliamentary secretary of how he thinks this provision is more equitable. I cannot see anything equitable about it. It seems to me that in the interests of progress, of removing our income tax rules from the medieval era in which women were not recognized for their efforts, in order to modernize the situation and give the legislation a truly progressive appearance, this kind of simple change would go a long way toward that end. I wonder if I could have an answer from the parliamentary secretary.
I want to point out, Mr. Chairman, that the parliamentary secretary was not even listening to the question and has made no effort to get up and answer it. I would like an answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I did listen long enough to ascertain that it was entirely fatuous.

Mr. Chairman, the charming parliamentary secretary has reached a conclusion and I was prepared to listen to his reasoning until he introduced the word "equity." This is where he hung himself. The hon. member for Edmonton West gave a very telling example of what could happen with the section as it now stands. A small businessman can take advantage of the act of incorporation, with his wife playing an important part in the business and able to receive income. The businessman, through the devious means of incorporation, would be able to charge off his wife's wages in computing his income.
Here we are talking about a husband and wife situation. But let us deal with another situation to which this principle has equal importance, that of man and wife in a common law union. I ask the parliamentary secretary not to bring in the red herring of what is a common law union.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Give us the ground rules.

You are the one who has to answer the questions. You are the one who is in government. I am throwing out these propositions in order to impress upon the parliamentary secretary that the use of the word "equity" was in error. A common law union is recognized in many instances in law as a valid union. I am not talking about paper and marriage certificates but about a union which is recognized in law. Reflecting upon the example given, the husband and wife involved in an incorporated company, and comparing that with the man and woman in a common law union, would the parliamentary secretary be prepared to admit that the word he used was wrong and that he should not have used the word "equity"? In fact, if he is going to talk about equity perhaps he should be amending that section to include the common law union.
I know that the government has wisdom, expertise and brains enough for its purpose with respect to this bill to defend it, and living under a common roof would be a good start. If we are to talk about equity, let us not be fatuous; let us be honest and change the section so that we have equity. As long as the situation remains as it is now, and as long as we and the parliamentary secretary can bring in the type of situation we have referred to, we can no longer talk about equity.

I would hope that the parliamentary secretary would use another word. I see the hon. member from St. Catharines wagging his tail and I don't know why.
Because you are barking.
That's a flipper; it isn't his tail.

Maybe the problem is money rather than equity. Would the parliamentary secretary be prepared to say that he used the wrong word, or is he going to stick with what he says here and what he is giving to the Canadian people and say that this is a situation of equity?
He doesn't understand it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I am not prepared to withdraw my suggestion that this is a question of equity. However, I think the government would be quite prepared to entertain any definition that the hon. member might care to propose-
I gave you a start.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -anything which would place common law relationship in a position relatively comparable to the family unit in more conventional circumstances. So far, achievement of that objective has defied our ingenuity, but I am sure the hon. member would be able to advance suggestions.

I am glad the parliamentary secretary dragged me into this debate by my heels, because I think he said it was beyond the government's ingenuity. That leaves me cold. As a matter of fact, it does not surprise me.
Hear, hear!

I would suggest, in all sincerity, that working in concert and in a spirit of co-operation with all the brains and expertise there is on the other side of the House and with the co-operation of this side of the House, it might be wise to stand this section. I know we are not playing games, Mr. Chairman.
Oh, oh!
There they go.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know who prevents members of the government from speaking. That is not my business, but I will have the opportunity to be on that side soon and I will find out. But surely when we try-
Come on over.
Things are better over here.

I will, any time you want to give up the reins of leadership. Your side of the House is extremely poor, so the Gallup poll says. We are prepared and have been prepared to take over. Let us get back to the subject. I was trying to make a good point. We have a responsibility here, gentlemen, and you are just wasting my time, your time and the time of the people of Canada.
November 9, 1971

Now that the parliamentary secretary is interested in equity, as we are, and is so interested in taking us under advisement, in a spirit of co-operation, and in view of the fact that he seems to have dug a hole from which he cannot escape, I ask humbly and in all sincerity-
Don't overdo it.

I am not overdoing it. Would the parliamentary secretary be prepared to say that I have a point? Would he be prepared to sit down and look into it further so that we might come up with an amicable and truly equitable solution? As he will not withdraw the word, would he be prepared to stand the section?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not the hon. member whom I would take under advisement-I did that some time ago-it is his ideas that I would like to consider, since he obviously has been giving a great deal of thought to this question in the several days it has been under discussion in the House. As a prerequisite to his request for standing a particular section I think he might wish to outline in detail the extent to which his ideas have developed.
Are you prepared to accept them?
Mr. Chairman, I do not believe the parliamentary secretary is taking me or members on this side of the House very seriously.
How can he?
I am trying to show to him, in all sincerity and honesty, that what we have here is not equity.
Right.
If he is prepared to accept my argument, then rather than being facetious-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I was trying to take the hon. member seriously.

I suggest that we should be serious and stand this section. The parliamentary secretary should not attempt to embarrass me by saying he would like to hear me develop my arguments. In the two or three examples which I gave, the parliamentary secretary should see that they show conclusively that there is no equity. If he is prepared to accept that, then I withdraw what I said about having him withdraw the word. Let us say there was some doubt, and I think there is. Would the parliamentary secretary be prepared to go that far? He is extremely difficult to convince but I know, Mr. Chairman, that he has compassion and understanding. I have seen him operate here in the past week and a half-
Don't make us cry.

-and when things become tough he is always prepared to say that we should stand this thing down and have another day to discuss it. I do not know why the parliamentary secretary cannot at least give us that courtesy. This section bothers members on both sides of the House, and notwithstanding the fact that those on the government side have not spoken I know they are as sincere as we are. All we want is an opportunity to look
Income Tax Act
into it further and see if we cannot work out a solution which we can call equitable. We may fail, but at least we would have given it the old college try. That is all I am asking and this is the last time I shall be on my feet regarding this matter. If the parliamentary secretary has at least some doubt he will agree we must stand it down until we look into it further. That is all I ask.
He had a heart when he was an ordinary member, but not any more.
He never had it then, either.

Mr. Chairman, I think I raised this matter originally about seven or eight days ago, and I am surprised that the government has decided, in the glowing words of the Prime Minister, that sex should be kept out of the bedrooms of the nation but it should not be kept out of the income tax law. I think members of the committee, including the parliamentary secretary, will recall that I said that the law which we have is so much hypocritical boloney, and I gather that the answer the hon. member for Hamilton West received tonight simply reinforces that point.
I shall make my points briefly. All we were trying to do in the opposition, and all we are trying to do now in regard to the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West, is to bring a little justice into the lives of very small people. These small people, in a sense, are the backbone of Canada, if you want to equate us with a nation of small people instead of large people and will a people who are prepared to work miserably long hours for miserably small returns and not feel that there is any economic bondage or servitude attached to that work.
The fact is that the section the hon. member for Edmonton West is trying to remove through his amendment is holding in servitude those people who earn less than $4,000 a year. It is as simple as that. I spoke a couple of days ago on this matter. I spoke on joint incomes-not on individual incomes but on joint incomes-which together come to less than $3,650 a year. We cannot bring justice to that group by passing the law as it is, yet the government's and the parliamentary secretary's intransigence prevent justice and the benefits of income tax reform being available to all Canadians.
We have somehow drawn a great big line and said that when two people live together and are married-and circumstances might be different if they were not married, but I will not go into that situation at this point; I will talk strictly on the amendment-and run a little business that does not earn enough to make it worth their while to incorporate, they will not get justice from the Parliament of Canada.
Shame.

Is that something we can be proud of? Can we hold our heads high? When I go home and talk to my kids I can say that if I have done nothing else this week, at least I have tried to do something in this area. I am not sure that we shall be successful, but at least I can hold my head high. At least the hon. member for Hamilton West and others on this side of the House can say, "We
