tried." However, since it is difficult to administer section 74(5) of the Income Tax Act we must all bow our heads before the great god of efficiency and say "On division" when we are asked to pass this subsection.
I submit that the failure, in the circumstances I have outlined, to give tax relief is a criminal abuse of responsibility. If we had any guts at all we would stand this section. The parliamentary secretary told me last week-I say this in all justice to him-that this is a matter that has bothered the income tax people for years and years and they were asking for a solution. If it bothers them that much, let us stand this section for another couple of weeks, pass everything else in the bill before us, in this 5-pound package of cure-all, and give people a chance to work on it We should tell some bright soul to work on this question on a 24-hour basis until he can come up with a hard answer. If we do not do that, we are not worth our salt as parliamentarians.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on this issue. Members of the opposition have made a heartrending plea for this section to be stood and to let somebody work on it on a 24-hour basis until a solution is found.
Hear, hear!

It may be that this problem came to the attention of certain hon. members just this afternoon even though they were active members on the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs at the time these problems were considered.
But they were not considered.
If they were not considered-

They were not
considered.
-I ask whether hon. members opposite felt that they had general responsibility to discuss this matter as long ago as 1952 or 1953 when this provision was first introduced into the act.
Let us discuss it as it now is.

It has been alleged that the government's failure to propose some sort of solution to the problem constitutes a criminal abuse of responsibility. What about the responsibility of the opposition? They are not proposing a solution.
Yes, they are.

So far as I have heard, they are not offering any formula for dealing with the very real problem of income splitting, which I admit raises problems of equity. I grant that there are inequities in the administration of the Income Tax Act. It is not a divine law, far from it. We all know that. But do opposition members honestly feel that if another 24 hours were spent on this section we would come forward with any solution?
The same argument applies to the other matter they have raised about the backbone of our country. I admit that there is a problem in the area of people who are

living common law. I wish there were some way to define the common law relationship so that it would be possible to give extra exemptions and benefits to people living in that state. But how is that to be done?
You are against those people.

The hon. member for Hamilton West has suggested that if we had any heart we would stand this section for another 48 hours and consider the matter. Does he think that in another 48 hours we could solve a problem that people have been thinking about for two decades without being able to solve? I do not think a further 48 hours will make much difference. I think people who suggest this are building up false hopes-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Is the hon. member for Athabasca seeking the floor?
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman. I thought the hon. member for Don Valley had concluded his remarks. I wanted to speak. However, since he still has the floor I will say no more.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was obvious to the Chair that the hon. member still wanted to speak. With respect, I think another hon. member should not seek the floor until the hon. member speaking has finished.
Mr. Chairman, I should be glad to hear from the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Athabasca.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Don Valley has accused the opposition of not coming forward with a solution. Obviously, he did not listen to what hon. members said during the past hour or so. It is equally clear from the answer the parliamentary secretary gave me that he was not listening either. He suggested that if you ask a fatuous question you will get a fatuous answer. I therefore want to explain in a little more detail, for the benefit of those on the other side of the House who have not been listening, what the situation is and what the solution ought to be. I hope they will co-operate.
The situation is this. If a man employs his wife, the tax structure penalizes him in that the wife cannot fill out a separate income tax return and declare her own income. She can only do that if she works for someone other than her husband. Let me give an example of what I mean. I will use round figures to make this simple. Suppose there are two businesses operating and they are across the street from each other. Let us say that they are not incorporated and that each business brings in a taxable income of $25,000 a year. In one case let us say that a man employs his wife and pays her a salary of $5,000 a year. You would expect that he would pay taxes on $20,000 and that she, in theory, would pay tax on the $5,000 that she has earned. However, the husband must complete his return to show that his income is $25,000. This means that the tax on the wife's $5,000, the income that is added to his income, is in the 50 per cent bracket.
Let us now suppose that through agreement these two businessmen employ the other's wife in their business. When those wives fill in their income tax returns they will pay income tax at the rate of 15 per cent or 17 per cent, or
November 9, 1971

whatever the case may be, on the $5,000 they earned. In each case there is a saving to the business of over $1,000. It is easy to see that this kind of provision has not been included in the legislation.
The government is not concerned about equity.
Nor with tax reform.

Why is that so? Would the parliamentary secretary explain it to me? I am not an expert on taxes- but I am greatly concerned about the ordinary man who is trying to make a living, and about his wife who may be interested in helping him get ahead and make progress-
In a family enterprise.

-in a family enterprise. Why does he think it is more equitable to make the woman who prefers to work for her husband pay tax of 50 per cent rather than 15 or 17 per cent, the rate which would apply in the example I have used? I do not think there is anything fatuous about that question.

Mr. Chairman, I rose rather slowly. I expected the parliamentary secretary to rise and answer the very clear, straight-forward question posed by the hon. member for Athabasca. The government worked for two or three years on this legislation. It brought in a white paper which was debated across the country. The main theme of it was equity. In fact, the whole concept of it was equity. The Minister of Finance has taken little part in this debate. Can he not understand it? Can he not defend this bill? I pose those two questions. Why is he not defending the equity that he so proudly boasted was the concept and purpose of the white paper?
Why could we not have a simple answer to the question posed by the hon. member for Athabasca? It was a simple, fair question. Where is this government that has concern for the average man? In 1968 they campaigned across Canada. They said there would be a just society for every man, woman and child, no matter what their financial status might be. The government has now dragged out the worn-out phrase that it is administratively difficult. Have they not heard of the computer? You feed in a question and you get an answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is that the way it works?

We are now getting a smart remark from the parliamentary secretary. They tried to project the administrative impossibility after the grain stabilization bill. That is an amazingly weak case they are building. When the minister in charge of the grain stabilization bill appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture he said it would cost $1.5 million a year to administer the program. Where can they stand on this question of administrative impossibility?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I am sure the hon. member will agree that his last remarks do not relate to the section before the committee. His opening remarks were preliminary but he is now referring to another piece

of legislation that was before the House. I do not think it relates to the bill before us and the sections being studied.

I rise to speak on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I and my colleagues would like to more fully understand the purport of Your Honour's ruling. Section 74(5) reads:
Where a husband and wife were partners in a business, the income of one spouse from the business for a taxation year may, in the discretion of the minister, be deemed to belong to the other spouse.
In the preceding section we were dealing with husband and wife businesses which are not incorporated and where income is deemed to be joint in the hands of one person or another. I think this is what the hon. member for Crowfoot was talking about. If I and my party are wrong on that, we should have some elucidation. This is an important principle. We thought we were squarely within the subsections of section 74.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I do not think the hon. member can ask the Chair to interpret the remarks of the hon. member in relation to a subsection which is being studied at this time. It was the impression of the Chair that the hon. member was referring to another piece of legislation. Perhaps I misunderstood.
In any event, the Chair has to make its own decision. I invite hon. members to stay as close as possible to the debate on the section before the committee. That is the only way the committee can make progress on this legislation. The hon. member for Crowfoot.
I think the hon. member for Don Valley is rising on the point of order. We want to kill as much time as possible. Let's hear him out.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Chair intervened to interrupt the hon. member for Crowfoot. If the hon. member for Crowfoot wants to complete his remarks, he may do so. It was not the impression of the Chair that the member for Don Valley was rising on a point of order.
I am not rising on a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I want to continue the debate.

Then I still have the floor. The hon. member for Don Valley has contributed much to the debate. There will be ample time for him to contribute and lend his wisdom to the debate when I have completed my brief remarks on section 74(5) with regard to unincorporated small businesses. I was dealing with the situation that was outlined very clearly by the member for Athabasca. Since that time the Minister of Finance has entered the chamber. He has not witnessed much of the debate and has contributed very little to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: You, too.
Well! We have a brilliant remark from the Minister of Finance. The minister wants to have this legislation passed by Christmas. A few more remarks like that and it may be next Christmas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Are you threatening Parliament?

Am I threatening Parliament?

I am trying to elicit a sensible comment from the Minister of Finance. Who am I, a lonely backbencher in the opposition, to threaten Parliament? How could I threaten Parliament? That was a ridiculous remark by the Minister of Finance. He could not threaten me with anything.
I was referring to the clear and simple example stated by the member for Athabasca. He referred to two businesses operating across the street from one another. Both were earning in the neighbourhood of $25,000. The wives worked for their husbands. The husbands could not deduct their wives' wages. They each have to pay income tax on $25,000. If they exchanged the work of the wives and paid them accordingly, they could each claim a deduction of $5,000. I am not explaining it as well as the member for Athabasca. I could take more time but I want to hear the reply of the Minister of Finance. He has now entered the Chamber and has shown a preparedness to make a contribution.
Before the Minister of Finance entered the chamber I said that he went across the country with the white paper. He said that equity was the principle of tax reform, to bring about equity was its purpose. The hon. member for Athabasca suggested that section 74(5) would not bring about equity for an unincorporated, small business. Surely the Minister of Finance cannot stand on the defence that it is administratively difficult or that it is not administratively efficient. We have had many things that are not administratively efficient, one of them being the Canada Pension Plan. Medicare may be another.
I referred to the grains stabilization bill but before I could get the words out of my mouth Your Honour cut me off in a way that suggested I should not get into that question. Far be it from me to get into a debate on that matter. The government admitted that the administrative costs would amount to $1 i million.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Again I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but I must remind all members that the committee is dealing with specifics. This is not the time for hon. members to engage in general debate. I realize that hon. members may have all kinds of opinions as far as these subjects are concerned, with respect to which hon. members might wish to question the policies of the government. The purpose of the intervention by the Chair is to help hon. members and to help the committee.

I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I shall not refer again to the grain stabilization bill. I had no intention of taking part in this debate until I heard the example set forth so clearly by the hon. member for Athabasca. The parliamentary secretary would not rise and say yes or no. It was a simple question. This bill is presented on the basis of equity. The hon. member for Athabasca showed that there were inequities produced by this legislation.
After I had risen the Minister of Finance suggested I had threatened the committee. I am surprised, Mr. Chairman, that you did not rise to caution him that this was not parliamentary language. I said, "Answer the problem.
(Mr. Horner.]
Answer the equation set forth by the hon. member for Athabasca."
Wait until you get the "blues."
Only cabinet ministers and the parliamentary secretaries get the "blues," Joe. You and I don't.
Oh, you may soon, when you take over from Baldwin.
The whole country gets Benson's blues.
Oh, oh!

Yes, the whole country suffers from Benson's blues. While I am speaking about the Minister of Finance may I say there have been rumours around that he is not going to run again, that he does not want to face the people after this tax bill. I do not know whether there is any truth in these rumours, but there are rumours that he will not run in the next election and that the Liberals will not have him as Minister of Finance after the next election, on any basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I do not wish to intervene unduly in the debate, but I think the hon. member should try to co-operate as much as possible. speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I will simply say that the hon. member opposite has tried to inpute motives to me. I have no motives. I am in favour of having good tax legislation in Canada, the best we can possibly have. I like to listen to members such as the hon. member who has the floor. He tries to shout very loud and it is often said to me that people who shout loudly really do not have much of an argument.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Here again, the Chair must say that this is not a question of privilege. These are only matters of opinion. I think the hon. member for Crowfood should be allowed to complete his remarks.
Mr. Chairman, I apologize. I did not intend to get into this debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have heard that one before.

Somebody said, "I have heard that before". I did not intend to impute any kind of motive to the Minister of Finance but I heard the remark he made imputing motives to me, first, and Hansard will bear me out. He felt I had no right to reply, no right to retort. I say the Liberal party will not have him as Minister of Finance when they go to the people in the next election because they cannot go to the people with this bill, a bill which is full of inequity, including this section 74(5).
The hon. member for Athabasca posed a simple question in a sensible, pleasant, quiet manner, one which exemplifies the character of the hon. member.

And of our party.
But the smug parliamentary secretary is afflicted with the dreaded disease of tunnel vision.
Oh!

I see you frown at me, Mr. Chairman, and wonder what this disease is. Perhaps I might be allowed to explain. Tunnel vision comes to those who have risen to such a position so important that they see only straight ahead; they do not see to the sides.

This tends to bring about a narrow view-

Mr. Chairman, I do not feel very good about the degeneration of the debate. The exchanges between the Minister of Finance and myself lend nothing to the debate, I agree, and I find the situation regrettable.

speechtext: Very well. Then talk about the bill.
I am quite upset by this situation. The minister again interjects and tells me to talk about the bill.
Hear, hear!

I intend to talk about the bill. I intend to talk about the bill for as long as I can or until the minister or his parliamentary secretary assure me that the question raised by the hon. member for Athabasca will be answered. Both the minister and his parliamentary secretary sit in their seats without answering the question. This is why I rose and said the question needed answering.
We are debating equity. We are debating the concept contained in the white paper. This bill is a by-product of the white paper and the discussion on the white paper. If we cannot get an answer in the House of Commons to a
Income Tax Act
simple question, then where can we get an answer? If we cannot get an answer in committee of the whole, with the tax experts before the representatives of the people, then where can we get an answer in a representative democracy?
Do not call them experts.

I am being kind and perhaps the good Lord above will forgive me for being too kind, but one has to be generous in this business. Since the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West has been ruled out of order, surely the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary can admit that there is a train of thought here that leaves a doubt in the minds of many citizens and should be resolved.
I want to see clause 74 pass as quickly as possible so we cam make progress, but in order to make progress we must have answers. That is a simple fact of life in a democratic society. In a totalitarian state where rule is autocratic, no one gets any answers; but in a democracy we should get answers, particularly when this House is in committee of the whole and the minister's two tax experts are before the people's representatives.
I shall say no more at this time, but I hope that the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary secretary answer the simple question put by the hon. member for Athabasca and answer it in a straightforward manner. Then I am sure we will make some progress. But if we start indulging in cat-calling we will never make progress, and I regret the Minister of Finance involved me in this sort of thing.

Mr. Chairman, I think the obvious riposte that comes to any sensible person on this side of the House is: No matter what the answer is, is it government policy? If it is, is it going to be changed? Whether this policy has existed for 10, 20 or 30 years, is it policy that is not capable of change? Are we stuck with the law of the Medes and the Persians which varies not and oppresses forever? That is really the essence of the question of the hon. member for Athabasca and the hon. member for Crowfoot. Before I died at the hands of the Canadian Press at three o'clock last Tuesday afternoon I can remember asking that question myself.
No matter what the law is, is it fair or unfair? The Minister of Finance is now in the committee and I would direct the question to him specifically so as not to waste time beating about the bush. The parliamentary secretary is simply trying to shore-up injustice or explain it away. I ask the Minister of Finance this question: Has the government reconsidered the position of husbands and wives within the framework of section 74 of the proposed Income Tax Act?
If it has, has the government decided that the old law should be carried on, or is it prepared, in light of some of the vigorous representations that have been made- though some of them were presented mildly and clemently, as in my case-to look again at the situation? Those are questions that I hope the Minister of Finance will answer. I do not Want to hear the old phonograph record played back by the parliamentary secretary; let me hear the voice of the government speaking to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would simply say that this is a very difficult problem with regard to which I have a great deal of sympathy. However, there is no way to deal with it unless you move to a family unit concept of taxation, and the government has freely admitted it is not prepared to so move. The reason is that it does not know what would happen and has not looked it through far enough. We admit that it might be possible to resolve the problem if we were to move to a family unit concept, but we are not prepared to do so because we do not know all the implications of such a move or whether we would be able to look at it in the future.
I said in my white paper and also in my coloured paper that was published afterwards that we wanted to study the problem further and deal with it some time in the future. I do not know how to deal with it at the present time, but I would very much like to hear some suggestions from hon. members opposite as to how to deal with the problem without creating great loopholes in the taxation system as presently constituted.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two on this question of administrative convenience. This is a concept that it is unpleasant for a government to put forward as a defence but I think one or two things can

be said for it and perhaps should be said at this time. I should like to remind hon. members opposite that when the white paper was first introduced-

It is quite true that if a taxpayer has a small capital gain it is very tempting not to include it in his income. The point, however, that this might create a temptation to evade taxation is well taken. The answer finally put forward in the revised tax bill is that the ceiling for capital gains was raised so that 90 per .cent of the capital gains-
What section is that?
Mr. Chairman, I said-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I would hope the hon. member would try as much as possible to co-operate with the Chair and the committee and relate as quickly as possible his comments to the section before us. The hon.
Income Tax Act
member is opening debate on the question of capital gains. Although we are looking at a very specific section, he has taken advantage of an answer that was given by the minister to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants and has pursued it a little too far so far as the Chair is concerned. I think he should return to the subject matter before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, the example I gave illustrates that the imposition of an arbitrary floor on that kind of exemption is an administrative convenience which works for the benefit of the taxpayer as it does for the revenue department. The temptation is removed, the consideration of eligibility is removed, and so on.
I developed that illustration because I think exactly the same principle applies to the question of income splitting between husband and wife. In effect, this bill and its provisions provide a floor on the splitting of income between husbands and wives. It will help to prevent taxpayers seeking tax avoidance. It will make it convenient for them and it will remove the consideration of determining what the appropriate income for the spouse is-and the spouse might as well be husband as wife-how many hours the spouse actually devoted to the business and what benefit the business achieved from those services. This is a simple instrument of administrative convenience with an element of equity. In the broadest sense it provides equity.

Mr. Chairman, I think it was long back that I raised the question originally or that the Minister of Finance raised the question with me. He asked what we on this side would do. The answer simply is that we would have accepted the amendment presented by the hon. member for Edmonton West. However, that issue is finished and he wants an answer. I say simply that what the government apparently has decided to do is to consider husband-wife transactions. Probably the amount of income tax that one could raise from that source would be very small.
I do not know how many husbands and wives would be in what I called earlier the mamma and papa proposition. On average, the type of transaction set forth in this section could not be too common. I would suspect the amount of revenue we are dealing with is under a couple of million dollars a year. For that we have taken the extraordinary step of condemning husband and wives to economic servitude as a unit. I do not think there is any common sense in the measure that was passed before. I do not know what Prime Minister was in office when it was passed. I am not pointing blame in that direction. All I do is look around and ask, why cannot we do better than this? Why can we not put a little sense into the laws that will not cause any problem to the national revenue department but will make life a little easier for people who run a business?
As I have said before-and I can prove it-these are businesses which on average earn less than $3,650 a year. That is not much of a return when one thinks of the return of the great taxpayers of the country. I do not think the country gets much revenue as a result of keeping this type of provision in the law and I do not think we get much of an answer when it is said that it is administra-

November 9, 1971
Income Tax Act
tively difficult to change the law. I am sure that it is administratively difficult to change anything.
Heavens above, a thought came to my mind but I suppose I should not follow it up. The point I make is that we hit the small people with this, yet we could take some of the load off their shoulders. We will not take anything great from the national revenue and I really cannot see why the government does not at least take a second look at the situation and try to do something about it. I would hope that that would be the case.

I judge that my earlier argument did not find much sympathy on the other side of the House. Let me try one other. There is no spouse in this country who does not contribute in some measure to her husband's earning process, whether he is on salary, whether he himself is employed or whether he is the owner of a business. If they live together and love each other and if they work together, she does something to contribute to his income-earning process, and this even applies to Members of Parliament-in fact, particularly to Members of Parliament.
If that self-evident fact is conceded in the House, then we come to the question of where to draw the line. Are they not arguing, then, on the basis of equity for an extra deduction for everybody who is married, because whether you are on salary, whether you own your business, whether or not it is incorporated, whether you work in the city or in the country, if your wife contributes to your incomeearning process why should she not get a deduction for it? Then we come back to the point that I made earlier. If we do not put a floor on the deduction which we will permit, which is in effect what we do through the requirement for incorporation, we get everybody into this act justifying deductions.
We would expect our bureaucrats, the employees in the Department of National Revenue, to look into every one of these relationships, to assess it and determine whether or not some benefit is justified, what the value of the benefit is per hour, how many hours are spent and what result is achieved. These are all questions that I think hon. members, however much they would like to see this deduction, must surely admit defeat the equity of their proposal.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, the problem is certainly one of equity under section 74(5). We are trying to find a solution, along with the government, to a very troublesome problem. The income group that we are talking about is not composed of the $25,000 a year man; they are not Members of Parliament and their wives but they are the small people who are running little entrepreneur businesses such as hot dog stands and small fruit stands where the husband and wife are of necessity forced into 24-hour service to the public. They have little or no savings with which to buy into the Canada Pension Plan which, everyone will admit, has some merit. They are not able to benefit from the Canada Pension Plan because, in a great many cases, between the two of them they do not have $800 clear profit from their small business. They are

eating off their own hot dog stand and they are feeding their children fish and chips out of the family bin. Those are the people about whom we are worried and for whom we want equity. They are in the thousands.
Look at the figures of Statistics Canada and you will find how many thousands of people in Canada have an income of between $3,000 and $5,000 a year which today, according to Canadian standards, is below the poverty level. Those are the people about whom we are worried. They do not benefit from the Canada Pension Plan but they are under the aegis of this act. They pay very small income tax, if any, it is true. But when you have a net income of $3,600 a year an extra $100 in income tax constitutes a serious problem. It may mean nothing to the $30,000 a year man. Perhaps he can afford to pay 46 per cent of his income to the three levels of government, but when you are below $5,000 a year and with a family you cannot afford to pay taxes of any kind to anybody.
This is the small but very significant group of people about whom we are worried, and sarcasm will not help nor will comments back and forth across the House. Passing this 707-page document will not help them either. Under section 74 (5) we have an opportunity to pool our common sense, if any, and to come up with a sensible, agreeable and equitable amendment. I assure you that it would not take ten minutes to receive approval from the House. There would be unanimous consent from this side of the House if the government gave some kind of relief to this group of people earning between $3,000 and $5,000 a year. It is these people, who have no net profit and who cannot benefit from the Canada Pension Plan, about whom we are worried. We have a problem here.
There is no one in the galleries and I do not suppose the press will bother to put this in the papers, but the members of this party are worried about the problem. I have been sitting here during the debate of the last two or three days and most of the remarks I have made have been relevant. None of them has been sarcastic and I hope some of them have been to the point. The people of Canada are fed up with the time we are wasting here at $25,500 apiece per year, plus expenses. We sit around here and waste the time of the country on a document which, it is admitted, needs more than 100 amendments. Let us on this side of the House who have the interest of the small people at heart get together and put forward an amendment.
Do you have all the wisdom over there? Let us have a bit of co-operation. Let us have some participatory democracy. I myself did not come from the upper class. I came from the working class and I have achieved this pre-eminence in the House through the support of people who now ask me, "What have you accomplished?" We have absolutely nothing in the way of co-operation from the other side of the House in respect of Bill C-259. Personally, I am ashamed of myself but I am not nearly as ashamed of myself as I am of sitting here with 150 government members who are not budging one inch. All we hear from them is sarcasm and loud remarks. I would have thought that in the great Liberal Party two or three members would have had the courage to say that perhaps there is something in what we say.

Hear, hear!
November 9, 1971

Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to speak again because of the poor reception my remarks received on a previous occasion, but there is one point that I believe has not been emphasized sufficiently with regard to the implications of section 74(5). I am referring in particular to the exemption that a working mother can now claim in respect of her children. If a married woman is a wage earner she can receive exemptions, which in essence are benefits, when computing her income tax. But if she is working for her husband, under the provisions of section 74(5) she may not be able to claim her wages as an exemption. I agree that this is a debatable question, but she also loses out through not being able to claim exemptions for care for her children.
A second look must be taken at this matter. In answer to some of the questions I asked, the parliamentary secretary said that this provision is the same as in the old Income Tax Act and has been in the legislation for years and years. But, Mr. Chairman, there is a provision in this bill whereby working mothers can claim exemptions when they hire what in essence are caretakers to look after their children. A working mother can claim so much per child as an expense when she hires a caretaker. This changes the complexion of section 75(5) to some extent from that contained in the old Income Tax Act.
In our society we have gone to great lengths to educate men and women. Up until now the Income Tax Act has encouraged highly skilled, married women to stay at home. As a result we lose the benefit of the money spent on providing them with their skills. Now this bill encourages those people to contribute to society through the use of their skills, and I wholeheartedly thank the minister, his parliamentary secretary and those involved in drawing up the bill for providing a basic exemption on a per child basis for day care. This may be claimed by a working mother or a working widow.
Our argument concerns the husband and wife situation. If they are in an unincorporated partnership the wife cannot claim the child care exemptions provided in this bill. But if their business is incorporated the husband can pay his wife a salary and she can get the basic exemption for child care expenses. Also, she can contribute to the Canada Pension Plan and become eligible for unemployment insurance. The question is: Are we striving for equity? Is it good enough to say that it is too complicated to achieve? I see the hon. member for Don Valley shakes his head negatively. That is not good enough for him, and it is not good enough for me.
Income Tax Act
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I would be reluctant to give the committee the impression that I agreed with anything that the hon. member just said.

I did not hear the hon. member, but it is not important. The whole purpose of the bill is to create equity. If the business is incorporated, the wife can claim the exemption. If it is not incorporated, she cannot enjoy many of the benefits that the bill will provide. This bill is providing for forced incorporation of small business, of the small, corner grocery store, the small laundry or drugstore, in the same way as it provides for forced incorporation of farming operations. Are we attempting to destroy family enterprise? Is that the aim? Through this legislation are we attempting to destroy family enterprise in the running of the corner grocery store, the delicatessen, the laundromat and the drugstore? Is this the purpose of the legislation?

Is this the aim, just as it is the attempt to destroy the small family farm? Does the government really mean to destroy family enterprise? These are the questions Canadians will ask all across the country. Having listened to the hon. member for Athabasca and to many other hon. members who have asked questions about this section, I can only conclude that that is the intention of the government.
Then vote against it.
It is a regrettable situation. I did not hear that remark, so I will ignore it. I would not want to accuse the hon. member of having tunnel vision once again.

maintopic: HEALTH-SHORTAGE OF CANADIAN-TRAINED MEDICAL DOCTORS AND PERSONNEL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
HEALTH-SHORTAGE OF CANADIAN-TRAINED MEDICAL DOCTORS AND PERSONNEL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over and over again during the last four years I have drawn the shortage of doctors to the attention of the House. On June 28, 1971, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) stated in the House that he expected there would be a meeting of the provincial Ministers of Health and that he would be making a full statement to the House on this matter.
On November 3, 1971, I asked the minister if he would make a statement to the House assuring the Canadian

November 9, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
people that the government was prepared to do something about the shortage of doctors and the importation of foreign doctors. In reply to my question he advised me to obtain copies of his statements outlining the very meritorious things that the government has done. This is why I have become concerned, because I have been receiving more and more correspondence outlining the difficulty people experience in finding a family doctor or getting medical attention of any kind. I have even had many members of this House speak to me about the problem.
The minister is reported as saying that it is the consumer, medical and health services, who are to call the shots for the doctor. Surely to goodness, Mr. Speaker, if that statement is correct it is time he got off his seat and did something about it. At another meeting he went further and said that health care was a clear citizen's right; in our society no citizen shall go without medical and health care because of his incapacity to pay or because of geographic location. Those are two statements that he made. The Minister of National Health and Welfare on another occasion stated that the shortage of doctors was a myth. What, really, does this government think? One day they have a shortage and the next day they have not. This was a headline in "Canadian Labour" in 1969. In "World Affairs" in March, 1970, it was stated that in 1961 there was one doctor for every 800 people. The article went on to state that the ratio is slipping and Canada now ranks twentieth in doctor-population ratio.
In the previous answer to my question on the "late show" the government said the situation was improving all the time. No consideration was given to the point that only half of the doctors in practice are general practitioners. Many are in administrative posts. I would like to know how many are employed by the government. Dr. Roberts, president of the CMA, and Dr. Evans and Dr. Creary of the CMA have pointed out the gravity of the situation in medical manpower.
Ask yourself if the government realized its responsibility when it introduced national medicare. The responsibility was to build medical schools, to supply teachers and equipment, to educate all those who wanted to pursue a career in medicine and a responsibility in foreign affairs to stop bleeding the poor nations of the world of their MDs. It is criminal that underdeveloped countries- poorer by every standard-who struggle to educate their young people to be doctors find them enticed away by rich countries such as the United States and Canada. India, Iran and Turkey have tried to put a stop to this practice and other countries will have to follow. What will Canada, who is currently using 50 per cent of the import doctors, do to fill the shortage each and every year? If this supply were shut off tomorrow, the condition of medical manpower would become very critical.
We have young men and women dedicated enough that they want to practise medicine. Over 600 fully qualified students were refused entrance to our medical schools because of lack of space to train them. We could not even train the most outstanding students. It is clear we have to step up our enrolment to take in students who are dedicated but who may not have grade B marks. It has been
[Mr. Rynard.J
pretty well proven that grades have little to do with the performance of the doctor after graduation. It is the person and his dedication that counts. Let us quit being hypocrites and robbing the underdeveloped countries of their doctors and at the same time piously proclaiming the foreign aid we give to them.
Why has not the government followed the Hall commission report to supply the necessary manpower? The report was quoted long and often when the national medicare debate was before the House. Why has not the government brought in other measures to help? When will the minister listen to the advice of experts? It is obvious that he does not know, he wanders in the wilderness, because one day we are short of doctors and the next day we are not. I hope the minister is never in the position of having to wait a long time in an emergency ward of a hospital for medical attention. It would certainly give him time to ponder, if the occasion arose, to contemplate just how overworked are the doctors in the emergency wards.
Two-thirds of the people seen do not have serious or acute illnesses but are there because they cannot get an appointment to see a good practitioner. Some people require immediate care but often they do not get it. This does not lead to good preventive medicine. The seriousness of some cases is missed and the doctor is simply being pushed mentally and physically, his work suffers and the treatment of the patient is not as good as it should be.
What, then, do we do to correct this situation? The government could, under the health resources fund, immediately make funds available to the universities and provinces in order to provide the medical centres that are required to train the doctors we need. If possible, 2,000 medical students each year should be trained. This ought to be a first priority.
A manpower survey of the incentives required for a doctor to spend his first five years in general practice should be carried out. Staff should be provided with which to run our expensive medical schools all year instead of only three-quarters of the time. If this is arranged gradually we will be able to provide the doctors and facilities needed to give a high level of preventive medical care, which would cut down on hospitalization care and prevent or delay the onset of many chronic illnesses. The Canadian people deserve no less from this government than the ministerial implementation of the provision of adequate medical care for all Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: HEALTH-SHORTAGE OF CANADIAN-TRAINED MEDICAL DOCTORS AND PERSONNEL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) about the shortage of doctors, I will say that the government's efforts to increase the number of doctors graduated from our medical schools in order to meet the ever increasing needs of health services have often been discussed in this House.
As the hon. member pointed out, he has brought this subject to the attention of the House many times in the past.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has often said that the doctor per capita ratio in Canada is one of the highest in the world; we believe that
November 9, 1971

the ratio recommended by the Royal Commission on Health Services should be passed soon.
The number of graduates or undergraduates in mede-cine in Canada cannot be as low as the hon. member for Simcoe North claims. We are looking for means of improving access to and availability of medical care for all Canadians. For instance, the Department of National Health and Welfare finances studies in order to find various ways of relieving doctors of some tasks by giving them to medical personnel able to perform those services. Moreover, projects are set up to have nurses accompany doctors in order to provide the population with mobile health services. Recently, a special committee prepared a program to improve the training of nurses working in northern Canada where they are responsible for many duties normally performed by doctors. Furthermore, following recommendations of the national conference of paramedical personnel, a committee has been established for the purpose of setting up policies regarding recruitment and training of nurses to work in doctor's offices and contribute to offering improved services.
Those are examples of tasks which can be carried out by persons other than physicians, and this is likely to improve services to the public.
The matter is a complex one, involving problems of training, of recourse to professions related to the health field and of issuing of licences, all of which are being attentively considered by the department, as mentioned repeatedly by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and an increase in the quantity of health services does not depend exclusively on the number of physicians. Furthermore, many professional organizations are studying the problem in Canada. There is agreement on the necessity of resorting to supporting medical personnel, on the best use of the staff in related fields and on improved use of the technology made available.
Both at federal and provincial levels and within professional health organizations, there is a constant concern with improvement of medical services in Canada.

maintopic: EDUCATION-DECREASE IN NUMBER OF GRADUATE STUDENTS FROM UNDERDEVELOPED COUNTRIES FOLLOWING CHANGES IN RULES RESPECTING CERTAIN GRANTS
EDUCATION-DECREASE IN NUMBER OF GRADUATE STUDENTS FROM UNDERDEVELOPED COUNTRIES FOLLOWING CHANGES IN RULES RESPECTING CERTAIN GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to ask a question about the problem of graduate students from underdeveloped countries studying in Canada at the present time. Canada has had a good record in admitting graduate students from underdeveloped countries, principally from Africa and Asia, and we have made a good contribution. At the same time, our country and universities have benefited from having in our midst these foreign students representing, as they do, the cultures of the developing countries.
At present, and unknown I think to most Canadians, a series of unrelated decisions by various levels of government has brought about a serious reduction in the number of graduate students from underdeveloped countries presently studying in Canada. I will enumerate three of the decisions of which I have been made aware. Perhaps there are others of which other hon. members have
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
knowledge. First, by recent decisions both the National Research Council and the Canada Council have determined that no grants will be made to students unless they are landed immigrants of at least 12 months standing in Canada. This, of course, automatically rules out grants to any student except one who decides to become a landed immigrant and, presumably, is electing to become a Canadian citizen.
Second, the Canadian International Development Agency has shifted the balance of its activity. The number of scholarships which it is offering to graduate students from underdeveloped countries has been reduced. The purpose is to concentrate more on assisting education in underdeveloped countries and to encourage students, both undergraduate and graduate, to complete their university work at home.
The third factor is one which prevails in the province of Ontario and which I have no doubt exists elsewhere in the country. At the present time, provincial regulations limit the payment which any university in Ontario may make to a graduate student to $1,800 per year. As a matter of general policy our immigration department advises all intending student visa applicants that they must have at least $2,500 to support themselves while in Canada. For students coming from Asia or Africa there is a further expenditure for air fare which will perhaps amount to $1,000.
As I said before, these students who might otherwise work in universities in Ontario cannot hope to share in any research grants from either the Canada Council or the National Research Council. The result of the three separate types of decisions which have been made in Canada in the last year is that there has been a drastic reduction in the number of graduate students from Africa and Asia studying in Canada. I have some unofficial figures from a university in Ontario. They indicate that the student visa component of the university population in the present year has dropped over-all by only 2 per cent. In fact, in this particular university the number of graduate students from the United States has increased by 50 per cent and the number of graduate students from the United Kingdom has increased by 100 percent. The overall reduction has occurred at the expense of graduate students from the underdeveloped countries of Africa and Asia.
As I said at the beginning, the rather catastrophic decline in the number of graduate students presently in Canadian universities arises from a series of unrelated decisions. However, it seems to me that it is of such a character that it invites the serious consideration of all levels of government. This is my reason for raising the question in the House of Commons.

maintopic: EDUCATION-DECREASE IN NUMBER OF GRADUATE STUDENTS FROM UNDERDEVELOPED COUNTRIES FOLLOWING CHANGES IN RULES RESPECTING CERTAIN GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) for having raised this question. From the information he has presented to the House it seems that there is cause for considering whether the joint effect of several of these isolated decisions, taken no doubt for the best of

reasons in isolation, may have some over-all undesirable results.
I cannot speak this evening for all the agencies mentioned by the hon. member, but I can say that as far as the Canadian International Development Agency is concerned there has been little essential change in the rules covering the requirements leading to the granting of awards for graduate studies in Canada to students from developing countries. However, in recent years there has been a de-emphasis on the standard fields of study, for example, the general arts degree, as universities in the developing countries increase their capacity to absorb more students in traditional areas of study.
On the other hand, there has been an increased emphasis on the granting of awards for training in specialized studies, some of which are not given in Canadian universities but, for example, in technical colleges, teachers' colleges and mining schools. I am sure all the other agencies of government will consider very carefully the representations which my hon. friend from Grenville-Carleton has made to the House this evening.

maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-EXPEDITING OF PROVISION OF SEVERANCE PAY TO LAID-OFF EMPLOYEES
PUBLIC SERVICE-EXPEDITING OF PROVISION OF SEVERANCE PAY TO LAID-OFF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 20 I asked two questions respecting severance pay for government employees who had been laid off through no fault of their own. The questions resulted from a meeting I held in Gimli, Manitoba, attended by some 60 former employees of the Canadian forces base there. Most of them, if not all, were encountering severe difficulties. Practically every one of them had been faced with problems concerning severance pay in one way or another,. I therefore asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) the following question:
Has the minister taken any steps to ensure that severance pay owing to former employees of the federal government who have been laid off is being provided to them much more rapidly than has been the case in the past in the light of the fact they must live on severance pay for a number of weeks before they can get unemployment insurance?
In reply, the President of the Treasury Board said:
My colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services has been conducting a review of pay operations in his department and one of the objects of it is to speed up this process to which reference has been made.
That reply is not good enough. It has been taking up to three months in some cases for employees of the federal government who have been laid off to receive severance pay. At present they are not eligible to draw unemployment insurance until a certain portion of this pay has been used up. This being the case, it is necessary that they receive severance pay immediately upon termination of their services if they are to have anything upon which to live.
I have suggested to the minister in a letter that perhaps a percentage of the severance pay could be paid immediately on severance, leaving the complicated calculation as to exactly how much individuals are to be awarded until later. I hope this suggestion is being pursued. However, that is not the main reason for my question tonight. My reason for speaking has to do with a related question

which I addressed to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey), that question being as follows:
Is the minister giving consideration to removing the regulation which treats severance pay as income for the purpose of calculating unemployment insurance benefits in light of the fact that a number of inequities have arisen from that situation?
In his reply the minister said he was not considering removing the regulation. I was glad to learn from the answer, though, that the department has recognized at least a small portion of the problem which has resulted from this regulation and is moving to correct it. I refer to the possibility that if a person lives on severance pay for more than 32 consecutive weeks he might be disqualified from drawing unemployment insurance for reasons which are too complicated for me to go into now. Once again that action, however welcome it may be, is simply not good enough. Severance pay should not be considered as income for purposes of calculating unemployment insurance benefits.
The first point to make in this regard is that severance pay is not specifically referred to in the act. Its inclusion as a type of income is the result of a regulation of the department interpreting the act. Those members of the House committee who studied the new Unemployment Insurance Act with whom I raised this question have expressed astonishment and concern that it should be so considered, and they said the idea that it might be so considered had not occurred to them. This suggests to me that in drafting the regulation which includes severance pay as income for purposes of calculating unemployment insurance benefits, the department may have gone beyond the expressed wishes of Parliament or, at least, misinterpreted them. That is point one.
Point two: In the case of the former employees of the Department of National Defence the new regulation contravenes the manual which sets out their conditions of employment-the "A and A Manual". It is specifically stated in that manual that severance pay is not to be considered as income.
Point three: Severance pay is available to Department of National Defence employees as a result of an agreement negotiated between the employees and their employer. The regulation thus, in effect by the unilateral action of one of the parties, the government, deprives de facto the other party to the agreement, the employee, of one of the fringe benefits mutually agreed upon.
Point four: Severance pay was obviously designed to compensate persons laid off for such effects of the lay-off as lost sick leave, reduced pension benefits, lost furlough leave and to help compensate for the dislocation which inevitably results from being laid off, and so forth. If recipients of severance pay must now exhaust all or a portion of that severance pay before they become entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, then it no longer constitutes such compensation. It no longer constitutes such compensation unless, of course, the person finds another job immediately, in which case he has the severance pay free and clear. Surely the discrimination which results from this situation-the difference in treatment which is in fact meted out to those who immediately find
November 9, 1971

work and those who do not-is sufficient reason to get rid of the regulation.
Point five: If the severance pay is to be considered income, and if the Unemployment Insurance Commission is to consider those in receipt of severance pay as being employed-and all have been notified to this effect-why [DOT] should not the time they are living off their severance pay be considered pensionable time, for example? It is not, and that fact is simply another example of the discriminatory aspects of the regulation and another reason for its being repealed.
One final fact. In March, when the employees of CFB, Gimli, were being acquainted with the action the government would be taking on their behalf once they were laid off, officials of the Department of National Defence promised them both severance pay and unemployment insurance to assist them over this period. They now find it is an either/or proposition-either severance pay or unemployment insurance benefits. I know they were not deliberately misled but they were misled none the less, and the lack of deliberation does not diminish in any way their resultant difficulties. Let us just get rid of the regulation in question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-EXPEDITING OF PROVISION OF SEVERANCE PAY TO LAID-OFF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall reply only to the question put by the hon. member for Selkirk
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
(Mr. Rowland) to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), as found at page 8859 of Hansard, and not to the one he put to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). I quote:
-Has he taken any steps to ensure that severance pay owing to former employees of the federal government who have been laid off is being provided to them much more rapidly that than has been the case in the past, in light of the fact they must live on severance pay for a number of weeks before they can get unemployment insurance? I mention in particular over 40 people from the Canadian Armed Forces base, Gimli.
The President of the Treasury Board gave the following reply:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services, has been conducting a review of pay operations in his department, and one of the objects of it is to speed up this process to which reference has been made.

I am informed that the process is that the employing department, in this case National Defence, is required to requisition final pay cheques, including severance pay. The Winnipeg office of Supply and Services was able to get out final pay cheques within 48 hours of receiving requisitions. There were some instances where the employing department failed to include severance pay in their cheque requisitions but these omissions have now been corrected.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.29 p.m.
